question.prompt: When the roots of the polynomial \[P(x) = (x-1)^1(x-2)^2(x-3)^3 \cdots (x-10)^{10}\] are removed from the real number line, what remains is the union of \(11\) disjoint open intervals. On how many of those intervals is \(P(x)\) positive?

solutions.title: Count negative odd factors
solutions.explanation:
Even powers are positive away from their roots, so only the factors with odd exponents affect the sign of \(P(x)\).

An odd power has the same sign as its base. Therefore, at every point remaining on the number line, \(P(x)\) has the same sign as
\[
Q(x)=(x-1)(x-3)(x-5)(x-7)(x-9).
\]
A factor \(x-k\) is negative exactly when \(x<k\). Counting these negative factors gives the following table; the even-numbered roots will be removed afterward.

| Range of \(x\) | Negative factors in \(Q(x)\) | Sign |
|---|---:|:---:|
| \((-\infty,1)\) | 5 | \(-\) |
| \((1,3)\) | 4 | \(+\) |
| \((3,5)\) | 3 | \(-\) |
| \((5,7)\) | 2 | \(+\) |
| \((7,9)\) | 1 | \(-\) |
| \((9,\infty)\) | 0 | \(+\) |

A product of nonzero factors is positive exactly when the number of negative factors is even. Hence the positive ranges are \((1,3)\), \((5,7)\), and \((9,\infty)\), except that the original roots \(2,6,10\) must also be removed. Each of those roots splits one positive range into two intervals:
\[
(1,2),\ (2,3),\ (5,6),\ (6,7),\ (9,10),\ (10,\infty).
\]
The table excludes every other interval, so there are exactly \(\boxed{6}\) positive intervals, choice \(\text{C}\).
